title: Reading strategies
subtitle: Features, skimming and the whole passage
summary: Read a passage the way the paper expects: use its headings and footnotes, skim it fast, and answer questions about it as a whole.

lesson.heading: 60 minutes, 40 questions, no extra time
lesson.text: The Reading paper lasts **60 minutes** and contains three sections with 40 questions in total. You must also copy your answers onto the answer sheet, and - unlike the Listening paper - **no extra time is given for that**. Each section is a little harder than the one before.

examples.text: **Academic:** three long texts of an academic nature.
**General Training:** a mixture of long and short general texts, plus work-related texts.

lesson.note: Decide which module you need *before* you enrol - they are two separate tests.

lesson.heading: How to spend 20 minutes on a section
rows: Read the passage as quickly as possible
Look at the questions to see what information you need to find
Read in detail and answer the questions
Transfer your answers, checking and filling any gaps
lesson.note: If a question is taking too long, move on. A question you leave blank costs the same as a question you get wrong, but the minutes you spend on it cost you other marks too.

lesson.heading: The passage tells you about itself
lesson.text: Before you read a word of the body text, use the passage's own features. The **heading** names the topic, the **subheading** gives you the context, and **footnotes** explain technical terms so you do not have to guess them.

examples.text: **subheading** - *Sid Cowans looks at the health properties of a favourite drink*
examples.note: The context: who is writing, and about what.

examples.text: **footnote** - *In chemistry, an alkali is the opposite of an acid.*
examples.note: A definition handed to you for free.

examples.text: **caption** - *Tannins exist in all types of tea*
examples.note: The point the picture is making.
The rest of the furniture - know the names, they appear in instructions.

lesson.heading: Predicting from the subheading

left.label: *Climatologists are assessing the impact of climate change on high-altitude bodies of water.*
examples: Expect research linked to trends in weather patterns.
Expect a description of a project in mountainous areas.

right.label: *Researchers disagree about whether social media is making us more isolated.*
examples: Expect arguments put forward by several different experts.
Expect a discussion about the impact of technology on society.

lesson.note: *Researchers disagree* promises several voices; *Alan Parker outlines* promises one. That difference decides what kind of questions can be asked.

lesson.heading: Skimming is not reading
lesson.text: Skimming means going through the passage quickly, concentrating on **content words - nouns and verbs** - to get the main points. You are not reading for detail. It also shows you how the passage is organised, which makes finding things later much faster. Aim for **100 words in 30 seconds**.

examples.text: Paragraph A - a list of factors that brought about changes in our diet
Paragraph B - a comparison of children now and in the past
Paragraph D - different hypotheses for the changes in weight

lesson.note: After skimming you should be able to say roughly *where* something was - near the beginning, in the middle, near the end - even if you cannot quote it.

lesson.heading: Some questions are about the whole passage
lesson.text: A **global** question asks about the passage as a whole: choose the best title, or describe the writer's tone. The right answer covers the *main* idea of the whole text - not one striking detail from a single paragraph.

examples.text: A good title covers every paragraph.
examples.note: *The rapid transformation occurring in children's body size* covers the diet, the comparison and the theories.

examples.text: A wrong title is usually true but too narrow.
examples.note: *The impact of modern technology on today's food production* is only part of paragraph A.

examples.text: Tone: *He is giving a neutral account of recent scientific research.*
examples.note: The writer reports the two theories without taking sides - so *shocked*, *enthusiastic* and *doubtful* are all too strong.

lesson.text: Spelling is marked in Reading too - and here the correct spelling is printed in front of you. Copy it exactly from the passage.

exercises.prompt: Match each feature of a Reading passage with what it does.
How long does the Reading paper last, and how much extra time do you get to transfer your answers?
options: 60 minutes, with no extra transfer time
90 minutes, with no extra transfer time
exercises.explanation: Unlike Listening, Reading gives you no extra time - budget 3-4 minutes per section for transferring.

exercises.prompt: In the exam you should aim to skim read 100 words in ___ seconds.
exercises.explanation: In your own language 100 words takes about 20 seconds. Thirty is the realistic target in English.

exercises.statement: Skimming means reading every word of the passage carefully before you look at the questions.
exercises.explanation: Skimming means going through it quickly, concentrating on nouns and verbs, to get the main points and see how it is organised.

exercises.prompt: Match each subheading with the type of information the passage will contain.

pairs.right: arguments put forward by several experts
research linked to trends in weather patterns

pairs.left: Alan Parker outlines a recent breakthrough
pairs.right: an argument presented from one expert's point of view

pairs.left: A schoolgirl helped turn soap into an $18 billion industry
pairs.right: a historical look at a successful business venture

exercises.prompt: A passage compares children's diets and activity in 1970 and 2010, then sets out two competing theories. Which title fits best?
options: Children's eating patterns mimic those of their parents
The rapid transformation occurring in children's body size
A demonstrated positive link between diet and health in children
The impact of modern technology on today's food production
exercises.explanation: A global question needs the idea that covers every paragraph. The other three are each true of one part of the text at most.

exercises.prompt: You have 20 minutes for one section. Sort these tasks by when they belong.

items.text: Look at the questions to see what to find
Transfer your answers and fill any gaps

exercises.prompt: The writer reports two competing theories about childhood obesity without supporting either. What is the tone?
options: A neutral account of recent scientific research
Shock that so many children are overweight
Enthusiasm about the progress being made
Doubt that the situation will change
exercises.explanation: Reporting both sides without taking one is neutral. Strong feeling words need strong evidence in the text.

exercises.prompt: A note at the bottom of the passage explaining a technical term is called a ___.
exercises.explanation: Footnotes are there to help. Check for them before you spend a minute guessing a word from context.

exercises.statement: If a question is taking too long, you should stay with it until you solve it.
exercises.explanation: Move on. Every minute spent on one stubborn question is a minute taken from questions you could answer easily.
